name: Limit
quick: A value approached by nearby outputs.
definition: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ means outputs approach $L$ as inputs approach $a$ through nearby domain points other than $a$.
confusion: A limit need not equal the function value.
section: Approaching a value from nearby inputs

name: One-sided limit
quick: A limit using inputs on one side.
definition: The superscripts $a^-$ and $a^+$ restrict approach to inputs below or above $a$.
confusion: Different one-sided limits do not average into a two-sided limit.
section: Approaching a value from nearby inputs

name: Indeterminate form
quick: A substitution pattern that does not settle a limit.
definition: The symbol $0/0$ records vanishing numerator and denominator, not a valid quotient.
confusion: Indeterminate does not mean nonexistent.

name: Squeeze theorem
quick: Matching bounds determine a limit.
definition: If $g\le f\le h$ near $a$ and both bounds tend to $L$, then $f$ tends to $L$.
confusion: The bounds must approach the same value.

name: Vertical asymptote
quick: A vertical line approached with unbounded output.
definition: The line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote if a one-sided limit at $a$ is infinite.
confusion: A removable hole is not a vertical asymptote.
section: Unbounded behavior and limits at infinity

name: Limit at infinity
quick: Long-run output as inputs grow without bound.
definition: $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L$ means outputs stay close to $L$ for sufficiently large inputs.
confusion: An infinite input limit can have a finite output limit.
section: Unbounded behavior and limits at infinity

name: Continuity
quick: The nearby limit equals the actual value.
definition: At an interior point, continuity means $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$ with both sides defined.
example: Setting the missing value of $(x^2-16)/(x-4)$ to $8$ repairs continuity.
confusion: Existence of a limit alone does not establish continuity.
section: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

name: Intermediate value theorem
quick: A continuous function takes intermediate output values.
definition: A function continuous on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
example: Opposite signs of a continuous polynomial at $1$ and $2$ guarantee a root between them.
confusion: The theorem gives existence, not uniqueness.
section: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

name: Epsilon–delta guarantee
quick: Every output tolerance has a uniform input tolerance.
definition: For each $\epsilon>0$, choose $\delta>0$ making $0<|x-a|<\delta$ imply $|f(x)-L|<\epsilon$.
confusion: Delta may depend on epsilon, but not on the subsequently chosen input.
section: A precise guarantee with epsilon and delta

name: Punctured neighborhood
quick: Nearby inputs excluding the center.
definition: The condition $0<|x-a|<\delta$ excludes $a$ but includes inputs on both sides within distance $\delta$.
confusion: Excluding the center is deliberate, not a missing case.
section: A precise guarantee with epsilon and delta

name: Average rate of change
quick: Output change divided by input change.
definition: For $a\ne b$, the average rate is $(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$.
confusion: Use changes in both numerator and denominator.

name: Secant line
quick: A line through two graph points.
definition: Its slope compares the outputs at two distinct inputs.
example: The secant of $x^2$ through inputs $1$ and $3$ has slope $4$.
confusion: A secant need not have the same slope as a tangent at either endpoint.

name: Derivative at a point
quick: A finite limiting difference quotient.
definition: $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}[f(a+h)-f(a)]/h$ when the finite limit exists.
example: For $f(x)=x^2$, the quotient at $2$ is $4+h$, so $f'(2)=4$.
confusion: The definition takes a limit; it never divides by a zero increment.

name: Derivative function
quick: The function assigning a slope to each eligible input.
definition: $f'$ maps $x$ to the derivative of $f$ at $x$, wherever that derivative exists.
confusion: The output of the derivative is a rate, not the original height.

name: Second derivative
quick: The derivative of the first derivative.
definition: $f''=(f')'$ measures how the first-order rate changes.
confusion: It is not the square of the first derivative.

name: Tangent line
quick: The line matching a function value and finite derivative.
definition: At $a$, its equation is $y=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$.
confusion: A tangent can cross the graph.

name: Velocity and speed
quick: Velocity is signed; speed is its magnitude.
definition: For position $s(t)$, velocity is $s'(t)$ and speed is $|s'(t)|$.
example: Velocity $-3$ meters per second corresponds to speed $3$ meters per second.
confusion: Negative velocity does not mean negative speed.

name: Differentiability
quick: Existence of a finite derivative.
definition: At an interior point, the two-sided difference quotient must converge to a finite real number.
example: $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$ because its one-sided slopes differ.
confusion: Continuity is necessary but not sufficient.

name: Corner
quick: A continuous join with unequal finite one-sided slopes.
definition: A corner prevents the ordinary derivative at the join.
example: $|x|$ has slopes $-1$ and $1$ at zero from opposite sides.
confusion: Do not average the slopes to invent a derivative.

name: Power rule
quick: Differentiate a power by multiplying by its exponent.
definition: $(d/dx)x^n=nx^{n-1}$ at inputs where the stated power is differentiable.
confusion: The exponent decreases by one; the function is not divided by its exponent.

name: Linearity of differentiation
quick: Sums and constant factors pass through differentiation.
definition: $(af+bg)'=af'+bg'$ for fixed real constants $a,b$.
confusion: Linearity is not a rule for products of variable functions.

name: Fractional-power derivative
quick: The power rule with explicit real-domain conditions.
definition: For rational $r$, $(x^r)'=rx^{r-1}$ wherever the real power is differentiable.
confusion: Endpoints and negative inputs require checking the real domain.

name: Product rule
quick: Differentiate each factor once and add the contributions.
definition: $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ for differentiable factors.
confusion: The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives.

name: Quotient rule
quick: A difference of cross-products over the squared denominator.
definition: $(f/g)'=(f'g-fg')/g^2$ where $g\ne0$.
confusion: The subtraction order and original denominator restriction both matter.

name: Radian trigonometric derivatives
quick: Standard trigonometric rates assume radian input.
definition: $(\sin x)'=\cos x$ and $(\cos x)'=-\sin x$ with angles in radians.
example: The slope of $\sin x$ at $0$ is $1$.
confusion: Degree input introduces a conversion factor.

name: Reciprocal trigonometric functions
quick: Secant and cosecant are reciprocals.
definition: $\sec x=1/\cos x$, $\csc x=1/\sin x$, and $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$ on their domains.
confusion: Reciprocal functions are not inverse functions such as arcsine.

name: Chain rule
quick: Multiply local rates along a composition.
definition: $[f(g(x))]'=f'(g(x))g'(x)$ when the required derivatives exist.
confusion: Evaluate the outer derivative at the inner value and retain the inner derivative.

name: Inner and outer functions
quick: The stages of a composition.
definition: In $f(g(x))$, $g$ is applied first and $f$ second.
example: For $\sin(x^2)$, the inner function squares and the outer function takes sine.
confusion: Composition is not multiplication of the functions.

name: Dependency chain
quick: The ordered stages connecting input to output.
definition: Each differentiable stage contributes a local derivative evaluated at its own input.
confusion: Count stages rather than applying one rule to the entire expression indiscriminately.

name: Implicit differentiation
quick: Differentiate an equation while preserving dependence.
definition: When $y=y(x)$, differentiating a term such as $y^2$ gives $2y\,y'$.
confusion: The dependent variable contributes chain-rule factors.

name: Local branch
quick: A portion of a curve representable as a function nearby.
definition: An implicit curve can admit a differentiable $y(x)$ near a point without being one global function of $x$.
example: A circle has upper and lower function branches away from its vertical extremes.
confusion: A global relation may contain several branches.

name: Inverse derivative
quick: Reciprocal slope at the corresponding original input.
definition: If $f(a)=b$ and the local inverse hypotheses hold with $f'(a)\ne0$, then $(f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(a)$.
example: If $f(2)=10$ and $f'(2)=13$, the inverse derivative at $10$ is $1/13$.
confusion: The reciprocal uses the matching original input, not the inverse input.

name: Principal branch
quick: A chosen one-to-one restriction defining an inverse.
definition: Arcsine uses the sine restriction to $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
example: $\arcsin(0)=0$, although infinitely many angles have sine zero.
confusion: Branch choices determine signs in inverse derivative calculations.

name: Inverse trigonometric derivative
quick: The rate of a principal inverse angle function.
definition: $(\arcsin x)'=1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$, $(\arccos x)'=-1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$, and $(\arctan x)'=1/(1+x^2)$ on their differentiability domains.
confusion: Arcsine is not cosecant.

name: Natural exponential
quick: The exponential whose derivative equals itself.
definition: $(e^x)'=e^x$; composition adds the inner derivative.
confusion: Do not lower the exponent as if applying the power rule.

name: Logarithm derivative rule
quick: Inner rate divided by inner value.
definition: $[\ln u]'=u'/u$ when $u>0$; $[\ln|u|]'=u'/u$ when $u\ne0$.
confusion: The derivative formula does not erase the logarithm domain.

name: General-base exponential derivative
quick: A fixed base contributes its natural logarithm.
definition: $(a^{u(x)})'=a^{u(x)}\ln(a)u'(x)$ for fixed $a>0$.
confusion: A variable base needs a different argument.
section: Other bases and valid logarithm identities

name: Change of logarithm base
quick: Convert a logarithm into natural logarithms.
definition: $\log_a x=\ln x/\ln a$ for $x>0$, $a>0$, $a\ne1$.
confusion: The denominator depends on the base, not on a variable exponent.
section: Other bases and valid logarithm identities

name: Logarithmic differentiation
quick: Differentiate a logarithm, then recover the original rate.
definition: For a positive $y(x)$, first calculate $(\ln y)'=y'/y$, then multiply by $y$.
confusion: Stopping at the logarithmic derivative omits a factor of the original function.

name: Variable power
quick: An expression with both base and exponent varying.
definition: For $u>0$, $u^v=e^{v\ln u}$, so both $u'$ and $v'$ can contribute.
confusion: Do not apply a fixed-base or fixed-exponent rule alone.

name: Relative rate of change
quick: Absolute rate divided by current value.
definition: For a positive differentiable quantity $P$, the relative rate is $P'/P=(\ln P)'$.
example: If $P=80e^{0.03t}$, the relative rate is $0.03$ per time unit.
confusion: An instantaneous relative rate is not an exact finite percentage change.

name: Doubling time and half-life
quick: Times to multiply an exponential amount by two or one-half.
definition: For constant growth rate $k>0$, doubling time is $\ln2/k$; for decay magnitude $c>0$, half-life is $\ln2/c$.
example: The model $P_0e^{-(\ln2)t/5}$ halves every $5$ time units.
confusion: These constant times are properties of the exponential model.

name: Logistic sensitivity
quick: The slope of a bounded exponential transformation.
definition: For $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$, $\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)=e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^2$.
confusion: Equivalent formulas can emphasize different properties without changing the rate.

name: Logarithmic penalty
quick: A logarithm-based quantity sensitive near a zero input.
definition: For $L(p)=-\ln p$ with $p>0$, $L'(p)=-1/p$.
confusion: The input must remain positive; zero is not a finite penalty value.

name: Related rates
quick: Rates linked by a shared equation.
definition: Differentiate a relation among time-dependent quantities with respect to the same time variable.
confusion: A value at one instant is not a constant throughout the process.

name: Signed rate
quick: A rate carrying its direction of change.
definition: A positive derivative denotes increase of the chosen quantity; a negative one denotes decrease.
example: A shrinking width can have $w'=-1/2$ meters per minute.
confusion: Do not replace a decreasing rate by its positive magnitude.

name: Geometric rate relation
quick: A geometric formula differentiated in time.
definition: For a sphere, $V'=4\pi r^2r'$.
example: Fixed inflow produces a radius rate inversely proportional to $r^2$.
confusion: Area rates and volume rates have different units.

name: Similarity constraint
quick: A ratio that remains valid throughout a changing shape.
definition: Similar cross-sections can relate changing dimensions before differentiation.
example: A cone with total radius-to-height ratio $1/2$ has $r=h/2$ for its water surface.
confusion: A persistent relation can be substituted early; an instantaneous measurement cannot.

name: Moving distance constraint
quick: A relation linking changing coordinate distances.
definition: From $d^2=x^2+y^2$, differentiation gives $dd'=xx'+yy'$.
example: Both horizontal and vertical motion can contribute to a separation rate.
confusion: Using only one coordinate rate ignores part of the motion.

name: Angular rate
quick: The derivative of an angle with respect to time.
definition: Trigonometric rate formulas use radians per time unit.
confusion: Angle units affect the derivative scale.

name: Linearization
quick: The tangent-based local model of a function.
confusion: A linearization is generally approximate away from the anchor.

name: First-order approximation error
quick: Error small relative to the input increment.
definition: Differentiability gives $[f(a+h)-f(a)-f'(a)h]/h\to0$.
confusion: Small absolute error alone is a weaker statement.

name: Differential
quick: The linear part of a predicted output change.
definition: With chosen $dx$, define $dy=f'(x)dx$; compare it with the actual $\Delta y$.
confusion: The differential is generally not the exact change.

name: Relative error
quick: Error compared with the underlying amount.
definition: A first-order relative output change is $dy/y$ when $y\ne0$.
confusion: A linear error estimate is not automatically a rigorous maximum-error bound.

name: Rolle’s theorem
quick: Equal endpoint values force a zero interior slope under regularity hypotheses.
definition: Continuity on $[a,b]$, differentiability on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$ imply some interior $f'(c)=0$.
confusion: The conclusion can fail at a corner.
section: Rolle’s theorem and the mean value theorem

name: Mean value theorem
quick: An interior derivative equals the interval’s average rate.
definition: Under continuity on $[a,b]$ and differentiability on $(a,b)$, some $f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$.
confusion: It guarantees existence, not necessarily uniqueness or a midpoint.
section: Rolle’s theorem and the mean value theorem

name: Monotonicity from derivative sign
quick: A sign condition throughout an interval controls ordering.
definition: If $f'>0$ on an interval, then $f$ is strictly increasing there.
confusion: The conclusion must not be applied across a domain gap.

name: Derivative change bound
quick: A slope bound limits total change.
definition: If $|f'|\le M$ between $u,v$, then $|f(v)-f(u)|\le M|v-u|$ under the MVT hypotheses.
example: Sine changes by at most the magnitude of its radian input change.
confusion: A bound valid throughout an interval differs from a derivative known at one point.

name: Concavity
quick: How slopes change across an interval.
definition: Positive second derivative implies concavity up; negative second derivative implies concavity down.
example: $e^{-x}$ is decreasing but concave up because its first derivative is negative and second is positive.
confusion: Concavity is not the same as increasing or decreasing.

name: Inflection point
quick: A continuous graph point where concavity changes.
definition: A sign change of the second derivative across a continuous point can establish an inflection.
example: $x^3$ changes concavity at zero; $x^4$ does not.
confusion: A zero second derivative alone is only a candidate.

name: L’Hôpital’s rule
quick: Certain indeterminate quotient limits can be evaluated through derivative quotients.
definition: Under the rule's differentiability and nonzero-denominator-derivative hypotheses, $0/0$ or infinite-over-infinite limits can pass to $f'/g'$ if that limit exists finitely or infinitely.
confusion: This is not the quotient rule and does not apply to arbitrary quotients.

name: Growth comparison by limits
quick: A quotient measures relative long-run growth.
definition: If $f/g\to0$, then $f$ is small relative to $g$ in the stated limit, even when both grow.
confusion: Unbounded functions can grow at very different rates.
section: Infinite quotients and transformed indeterminate forms

name: Indeterminate power
quick: A base/exponent limiting pattern requiring further analysis.
definition: For positive bases, taking logarithms changes a variable power into a product whose limit can be studied.
confusion: Symbols such as $0^0$ do not assign a universal limit.
section: Infinite quotients and transformed indeterminate forms

name: Objective and feasible domain
quick: What is optimized and which inputs are allowed.
definition: An objective $f$ is maximized or minimized over a specified feasible set of inputs.
example: The minimum of $x^2$ on $[2,5]$ is attained at $2$, not at infeasible input $0$.
confusion: A derivative root outside the feasible domain is not a solution.

name: Critical input
quick: An interior domain input with zero or undefined derivative.
definition: Critical inputs satisfy $f'(c)=0$ or have no derivative, with $c$ in the original domain.
example: Zero is critical for $|x|$ but is outside the domain of $1/x$.
confusion: Critical inputs are candidates, not automatic extrema.

name: Extreme value theorem
quick: Continuity on a closed bounded interval guarantees attained extrema.
definition: A continuous function on $[a,b]$ attains a maximum and minimum.
example: Every polynomial has both extrema when restricted to $[0,1]$.
confusion: Open or unbounded domains need separate existence arguments.

name: First derivative test
quick: Classify extrema by slope-sign changes.
definition: Negative-to-positive slope gives a local minimum; positive-to-negative gives a local maximum under the continuity and nearby differentiability hypotheses.
confusion: A zero derivative with no sign change need not give an extremum.

name: Second derivative test
quick: Use curvature at a stationary input.
definition: At $f'(c)=0$, positive $f''(c)$ gives a minimum and negative gives a maximum under the local differentiability hypotheses.
confusion: Zero second derivative means the test is inconclusive.

name: Closed-interval method
quick: Compare objective values at all candidates and endpoints.
definition: For a continuous function on $[a,b]$, evaluate interior critical inputs and both endpoints to identify absolute extrema.
example: A cubic can have its absolute maximum at an endpoint even when it has an interior local maximum.
confusion: Compare function values, not derivative values.

name: Attainment of an extremum
quick: A feasible input actually achieves the bound.
definition: An approached boundary value is not an attained optimum when its input is excluded.
example: $x^2$ on $(0,2]$ approaches zero but has no minimum.
confusion: An infimum is not always a minimum.

name: Constraint elimination
quick: Use a persistent relation to obtain a one-variable objective.
definition: Solve a constraint for one variable and substitute it into the objective while preserving feasible inputs.
confusion: Different constraints can produce different optimal proportions.

name: Degenerate geometric boundary
quick: A limiting design with a zero dimension.
definition: A zero-width or zero-height shape may lie at the boundary of a positive-dimension model.
example: For $V=x(12-2x)^2$, both $x=0$ and $x=6$ give zero volume.
confusion: A boundary limit may aid comparison even when the degenerate design is excluded.

name: Profit objective
quick: Revenue minus cost over feasible production levels.
definition: $\Pi(q)=R(q)-C(q)$, and its derivative compares marginal revenue and marginal cost.
confusion: Maximizing revenue is not generally maximizing profit.

name: Squared-distance objective
quick: An equivalent minimization without a square root.
definition: Minimizing nonnegative distance is equivalent to minimizing its square because square root is increasing.
example: Distance from $(x,2x)$ to $(3,0)$ is minimized by minimizing $5x^2-6x+9$.
confusion: The squared value has different units from the distance.

name: Discrete candidate comparison
quick: Check feasible discrete choices after a continuous model.
definition: For a concave quadratic, compare the feasible integers adjacent to its real vertex.
example: A vertex at $7.4$ requires comparing integer choices $7$ and $8$.
confusion: Rounding alone is not a universal optimization method.

name: Riemann sum
quick: A sum of sampled heights times widths.
definition: For a partition $a=x_0<\cdots<x_n=b$, choose $x_i^*\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ and form $\sum f(x_i^*)\Delta x_i$.
example: Two midpoint rectangles for $x^2$ on $[0,2]$ give $1(1/4)+1(9/4)=5/2$.
confusion: A finite sum usually approximates the integral; it is not automatically exact.

name: Definite integral
quick: The common limit of increasingly fine Riemann sums.
definition: The number $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is the Riemann-sum limit when the largest interval width tends to zero, independent of samples.
confusion: The integral is a number when both bounds are fixed, not a family of functions.

name: Signed area
quick: Area above the axis minus area below it.
definition: For integrable $f$, $\int_a^b f=A_+-A_-$; total geometric area is $\int_a^b|f|=A_++A_-$.
confusion: A zero signed integral does not mean the function vanished.

name: Integral additivity
quick: Adjacent interval contributions combine.
definition: If $f$ is integrable across the intervals, $\int_a^b f+\int_b^c f=\int_a^c f$.
example: If the first two contributions are $4$ and $-1$, the combined contribution is $3$.
confusion: Additivity applies to sums of contributions, not products of integrals.

name: Net change
quick: Final quantity minus initial quantity.
definition: Integrating a rate gives signed change: $Q(b)-Q(a)=\int_a^b Q'(t)\,dt$.
example: A net flow of $-2$ liters/minute for $3$ minutes changes volume by $-6$ liters.
confusion: An accumulated change is not the final quantity until the initial amount is added.

name: Antiderivative
quick: A function whose derivative is the given function.
definition: $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on an interval if $F'(x)=f(x)$ at every interior point.
confusion: An antiderivative is a function, while a fixed-bound integral is a number.

name: Constant of integration
quick: The arbitrary additive constant in a family.
definition: On a connected interval all antiderivatives of $f$ have the form $F(x)+C$.
confusion: The constant is added; an arbitrary multiplier generally changes the derivative.

name: Accumulation function
quick: An integral with a moving bound.
definition: For continuous $f$, $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ satisfies $A'(x)=f(x)$.
confusion: The dummy integration variable is replaced by the current bound after differentiation.

name: FTC evaluation formula
quick: Evaluate an antiderivative at the two bounds and subtract.
definition: For continuous $f$ and $F'=f$ on $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$.
confusion: The rule requires an antiderivative valid across the integration interval.

name: Substitution in integration
quick: A change of variable that reverses the chain rule.
definition: If $u=g(x)$, then $du=g'(x)dx$ and $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du$.
confusion: The differential and every remaining variable must be transformed consistently.

name: Transformed bounds
quick: The old endpoints evaluated in the new variable.
definition: With $u=g(x)$, a definite substitution changes $a,b$ to $g(a),g(b)$.
confusion: Bounds belong to their integration variable; mixing old bounds with a new variable is invalid.
section: Changing bounds and checking the model

name: Integration by parts
quick: The product rule read in reverse.
definition: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$, where $du=u'\,dx$ and $dv=v'\,dx$.
confusion: The remaining integral must be evaluated; the product alone is not an answer.

name: Partial fractions
quick: Decomposing a rational function into simpler rational terms.
definition: After division if necessary, factor the denominator and solve a polynomial identity for the decomposition coefficients.
confusion: One fraction does not split by dividing its numerator separately by the denominator terms.

name: Power reduction
quick: Replacing even trigonometric powers with lower powers.
confusion: Squaring a trig function does not permit applying the ordinary power rule directly.
section: Products and powers of trigonometric functions

name: Trigonometric substitution
quick: Using a trig identity to simplify a radical.
definition: For $a>0$, $x=a\sin\theta$ simplifies $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ on $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$.
example: With $x=2\sin\theta$, $\sqrt{4-x^2}=2\cos\theta$ on the chosen angle interval.
confusion: In general $\sqrt{z^2}=|z|$, so angle restrictions matter.

name: Verification by differentiation
quick: Check a proposed antiderivative against the original integrand.
definition: Compute $F'$ and compare with $f$ on the stated domain; an initial condition needs a separate value check.
confusion: Matching at a few numerical points does not prove symbolic equality.

name: Area between curves
quick: Integrate the nonnegative separation of the boundaries.
definition: If $f\ge g$ on $[a,b]$, then $A=\int_a^b[f(x)-g(x)]\,dx$. Split where their order changes.
example: Between $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, the area is $1/6$.
confusion: Taking the absolute value after integration can lose area through cancellation.

name: Average value of a function
quick: Total accumulation divided by interval length.
definition: For $a<b$, $f_{\mathrm{avg}}=(b-a)^{-1}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
confusion: The average of endpoint values is generally not the average of a nonlinear function.

name: Cross-sectional area
quick: The area of a slice perpendicular to a chosen axis.
definition: A solid with slice area $A(x)$ on $[a,b]$ has volume $V=\int_a^b A(x)\,dx$.
example: Circular slices of radius $x$ give area $\pi x^2$.
confusion: Integrate an area, not a radius or circumference, when adding thin volume slices.
section: Volumes from slices, disks, and washers

name: Washer method
quick: Subtract the inner disk area from the outer disk area.
definition: A washer with radii $R\ge r\ge0$ has area $\pi(R^2-r^2)$.
confusion: The area is not $\pi(R-r)^2$.
section: Volumes from slices, disks, and washers

name: Linear density
quick: Mass per unit length.
definition: A rod with density $\rho(x)$ has mass $m=\int_a^b\rho(x)\,dx$.
example: Density $2+x$ g/cm on $[0,2]$ cm gives mass $6$ g.
confusion: Density and mass have different units.
section: Density and work from variable contributions

name: Work by a variable force
quick: Integrate the force component along displacement.
definition: For a force along a line, $W=\int_a^bF(x)\,dx$.
example: A spring with applied force $kx$ requires work $kb^2/2$ to stretch from $0$ to $b$.
confusion: Force times total distance is valid only for a constant force component.
section: Density and work from variable contributions

name: Accumulation model
quick: A whole quantity built from local contributions and an initial level.
definition: For a rate $r$, $Q(t)=Q(a)+\int_a^t r(s)\,ds$, while a density model integrates local amount per unit length or volume.
example: A queue's fluid model uses arrivals minus service as its net rate while the queue remains positive.
confusion: A continuous model may stop applying when a physical or discrete boundary is reached.

name: Midpoint rule
quick: Approximate each interval using its midpoint height.
definition: For equal width $h=(b-a)/n$, $M_n=h\sum_{i=1}^n f(a+(i-1/2)h)$.
confusion: A midpoint sample is not generally the average of the endpoint heights.

name: Trapezoidal rule
quick: Integrate straight-line segments between endpoint samples.
confusion: Interior heights receive weight two because they border two trapezoids.

name: Simpson’s rule
quick: Integrate quadratic interpolants over pairs of intervals.
definition: For even $n$, $S_n=\frac h3[f_0+4f_1+2f_2+\cdots+4f_{n-1}+f_n]$.
confusion: The composite rule requires an even number of equal subintervals.

name: Quadrature error bound
quick: A guaranteed maximum discrepancy under smoothness assumptions.
example: Doubling $n$ divides these bounds by four.
confusion: An upper bound need not equal the actual error.

name: Improper integral over an infinite interval
aliases: Improper integral over an infinite interval
quick: A limit of finite-interval integrals.
definition: $\int_a^\infty f=\lim_{b\to\infty}\int_a^b f$ when the limit is finite.
confusion: Infinity is not a real endpoint to substitute into an antiderivative.

name: Improper integral at a singularity
quick: Approach an unbounded endpoint using a one-sided limit.
definition: $\int_a^b f=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{a+\varepsilon}^b f$ when $a$ is a singular endpoint and the limit is finite.
confusion: A singularity inside the interval requires two independent one-sided limits.

name: Comparison for improper integrals
quick: Use a simpler nonnegative integrand to bound another.
definition: If $0\le f\le g$ on a tail and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges; divergence of the smaller integral forces divergence of the larger.
confusion: Being smaller than a divergent function gives no conclusion.

name: Truncation error
quick: The contribution omitted when replacing an infinite range by a finite one.
definition: For a nonnegative integrand, the omitted tail after $B$ is $\int_B^\infty f$.
confusion: A quadrature error bound on the retained interval does not bound the omitted tail.

name: Limit of a sequence
quick: A value approached by all sufficiently late terms.
definition: $a_n\to L$ means that for every $\varepsilon>0$, eventually $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$.
confusion: A long initial pattern does not establish eventual behavior.

name: Monotone convergence for sequences
quick: A bounded monotone real sequence has a finite limit.
definition: An increasing sequence bounded above converges; the decreasing/bounded-below version is analogous.
example: $1-1/n$ increases and is bounded above by $1$.
confusion: Boundedness alone does not prevent oscillation.

name: Partial sum
quick: The finite running total of a series.
definition: $S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n$; the series converges to $S$ when $S_N\to S$.
confusion: The limit of the terms is not the sum of the series.
section: Partial sums, geometric series, and telescoping

name: Geometric series
quick: Terms with a constant ratio.
definition: $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}ar^n=a/(1-r)$ for $|r|<1$.
confusion: The starting index determines the first term.
section: Partial sums, geometric series, and telescoping

name: Telescoping series
quick: A sum in which intermediate terms cancel.
definition: Writing $a_n=b_n-b_{n+1}$ gives $S_N=b_1-b_{N+1}$.
confusion: Cancel in a finite partial sum before passing to the limit.
section: Partial sums, geometric series, and telescoping

name: Term test for divergence
quick: A convergent series must have terms tending to zero.
definition: If $a_n\not\to0$, then $\sum a_n$ diverges; $a_n\to0$ alone is inconclusive.
example: $\sum n/(n+1)$ diverges because its terms tend to $1$.
confusion: The converse is false: the harmonic series has terms tending to zero but diverges.
section: The term test and integral test

name: Integral test
quick: Compare a positive decreasing series with an improper integral.
definition: For eventually positive, continuous, decreasing $f$ with $a_n=f(n)$, $\sum a_n$ and $\int f$ have the same convergence behavior.
confusion: The integral and series need not have the same numerical value.
section: The term test and integral test

name: Direct comparison test
quick: Bound positive terms by a known series.
definition: If eventually $0\le a_n\le b_n$, convergence of $\sum b_n$ implies convergence of $\sum a_n$; divergence of $\sum a_n$ implies divergence of $\sum b_n$.
confusion: The reverse implications do not follow.

name: Limit comparison test
quick: Compare the eventual scale of positive terms.
definition: If $a_n,b_n>0$ and $a_n/b_n\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, both series have the same convergence behavior.
confusion: A ratio limit of zero or infinity is not the positive finite version of this theorem.

name: Alternating-series test
quick: Decreasing magnitudes tending to zero make alternating sums converge.
definition: If $b_n\ge0$ decreases to zero, then $\sum(-1)^{n+1}b_n$ converges and $|R_N|\le b_{N+1}$.
example: The alternating harmonic remainder after $N$ terms is at most $1/(N+1)$.
confusion: Alternation alone is insufficient without the magnitude conditions.

name: Absolute convergence
quick: Convergence after replacing every term by its magnitude.
definition: $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely when $\sum|a_n|$ converges. Absolute convergence implies convergence.
confusion: A convergent series whose absolute series diverges is conditionally convergent.

name: Ratio test
quick: Compare successive term magnitudes.
definition: If $L=\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|$, then $L<1$ implies absolute convergence, $L>1$ implies divergence, and $L=1$ is inconclusive.
confusion: A ratio limit of one does not establish divergence.
section: Ratio and root tests, with method selection

name: Root test
quick: Measure the exponential scale of term magnitudes.
definition: If $L=\lim\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}$, the same below-one/above-one/inconclusive-at-one conclusions hold.
confusion: Take the absolute value before an even root of a signed term.
section: Ratio and root tests, with method selection

name: Power series
quick: A series of powers around a chosen center.
definition: A power series centered at $a$ has form $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(x-a)^n$.
confusion: The center is determined by the power factor, not by the coefficient index.

name: Radius of convergence
quick: Distance from the center within which absolute convergence holds.
definition: A radius $R$ gives convergence for $|x-a|<R$ and divergence for $|x-a|>R$; endpoints need separate tests.
example: $\sum x^n/n$ has radius $1$, with different behavior at the two endpoints.
confusion: The radius alone does not determine whether boundary points are included.

name: Taylor polynomial
quick: A polynomial matching derivatives at a center.
confusion: The coefficient of $(x-a)^k$ is the derivative divided by $k!$.

name: Maclaurin polynomial
quick: A Taylor polynomial centered at zero.
confusion: Maclaurin names a center choice, not a separate approximation principle.

name: Taylor series
quick: The infinite series of derivative-matching coefficients.
definition: The Taylor series at $a$ is $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f^{(n)}(a)(x-a)^n/n!$. Equality to $f$ requires its remainder to tend to zero.
confusion: Having derivatives of every order does not by itself prove equality to the Taylor series.

name: Termwise calculus for power series
quick: Differentiate or integrate each term inside the radius.
definition: Inside a positive convergence radius, differentiation and integration preserve the radius; endpoint behavior may change.
confusion: Endpoint convergence must be checked again after differentiation or integration.

name: Taylor remainder
quick: The difference between a function and its Taylor polynomial.
definition: If $|f^{(N+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $a$ and $x$, then $|f(x)-P_N(x)|\le M|x-a|^{N+1}/(N+1)!$.
example: For $e^x$ near zero, bound the next derivative by an upper bound for $e^t$ on the interval.
confusion: The derivative bound must hold throughout the interval between center and target, not just at the center.

name: Leading-term analysis
quick: Use the first noncancelled power while controlling the remainder.
definition: If $f(x)=ax^k+o(x^k)$ with $a\ne0$, the ratio $f(x)/x^k$ tends to $a$.
example: $\sin x-x=-x^3/6+o(x^3)$ gives a limit of $-1/6$ after division by $x^3$.
confusion: Cancelling low-order terms requires retaining enough higher-order terms to determine the result.
section: Using series for limits and integrals

name: multivariable domain
quick: The permitted ordered input tuples of a function of several variables.
definition: The permitted ordered input tuples of a function of several variables.
example: For $\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}$ the domain is the closed unit disk.
confusion: The domain is a set of input pairs, not a set of output heights.

name: level curve
quick: The set of input pairs giving one specified output value.
definition: The set of input pairs giving one specified output value.
example: The level $c=4$ of $x^2+y^2$ is a circle of radius two.
confusion: Fixing an input produces a slice; fixing the output produces a level set.

name: multivariable limit
quick: A common output approached along every sufficiently close permitted input path.
definition: A common output approached along every sufficiently close permitted input path.
example: Different limits along $y=0$ and $y=x$ disprove a planar limit.
confusion: Agreement along sampled paths is not proof of a limit.

name: partial derivative
quick: The rate of change in one input while the other inputs are held fixed.
definition: The rate of change in one input while the other inputs are held fixed.
confusion: Holding y fixed does not mean substituting y=0.
section: Partial derivatives hold other inputs fixed

name: coordinate partials versus differentiability
quick: Coordinate partial derivatives alone do not guarantee continuity or a multivariable linear approximation.
definition: Coordinate partial derivatives alone do not guarantee continuity or a multivariable linear approximation.
example: With value zero at the origin, $xy/(x^2+y^2)$ has zero coordinate partials there but is discontinuous.
confusion: Continuous first partials near a point are a sufficient condition, not the definition of differentiability.

name: multivariable differentiability
quick: A single linear approximation whose error is negligible relative to every small input displacement.
definition: A single linear approximation whose error is negligible relative to every small input displacement.
example: For a quadratic, the remainder after linearization is of second order in the displacement.
confusion: Two existing partial derivatives identify a candidate linear approximation but do not validate its remainder.
section: One approximation for every small displacement

name: total differential
quick: The first-order output change obtained by applying the derivative to an input displacement.
definition: The first-order output change obtained by applying the derivative to an input displacement.
confusion: A differential approximates a finite change; it need not equal it.

name: gradient
quick: The vector of first partial derivatives of a scalar function in input-coordinate order.
definition: The vector of first partial derivatives of a scalar function in input-coordinate order.
confusion: A zero gradient is a stationary-point condition, not a certificate of a minimum.

name: directional derivative
quick: The local rate of change per unit distance in a specified unit direction.
definition: The local rate of change per unit distance in a specified unit direction.
example: For gradient $(3,4)$, the greatest unit-direction rate is five.
confusion: Normalize a supplied direction vector unless the question explicitly asks for a parameterized path rate.

name: regular level curve
quick: A smooth level curve near a point with nonzero gradient; its tangent directions are perpendicular to the gradient.
definition: A smooth level curve near a point with nonzero gradient; its tangent directions are perpendicular to the gradient.
example: At $(2,1)$ on $x^2+2y^2=6$, a tangent direction is $(1,-1)$.
confusion: The normal-direction conclusion needs a nonzero gradient.

name: total path derivative
quick: The derivative of a scalar output along a parameterized input path, including every changing coordinate.
definition: The derivative of a scalar output along a parameterized input path, including every changing coordinate.
confusion: A partial derivative along one coordinate is not generally the rate along a moving path.
section: A moving input changes several coordinates

name: dependency path
quick: A route through intermediate variables along which local derivatives multiply in the chain rule.
definition: A route through intermediate variables along which local derivatives multiply in the chain rule.
example: For $w=(u+v)^2$, both paths through u and v contribute to a changing input.
confusion: Products belong along paths; separate paths contribute by addition.

name: Jacobian matrix
quick: The matrix of partial derivatives, with outputs indexing rows and inputs indexing columns.
definition: The matrix of partial derivatives, with outputs indexing rows and inputs indexing columns.
example: A map from two inputs to three outputs has a three-by-two Jacobian.
confusion: A scalar gradient column is the transpose of the scalar function’s Jacobian row.
section: The Jacobian is the derivative matrix

name: Jacobian chain rule
quick: The derivative of a composition is the outer Jacobian at the intermediate point times the inner Jacobian.
definition: The derivative of a composition is the outer Jacobian at the intermediate point times the inner Jacobian.
confusion: The outer derivative must be evaluated at the intermediate output, not the original input.

name: implicit differentiation in several variables
quick: Differentiation of a relation along its locally defined dependent-variable path.
definition: Differentiation of a relation along its locally defined dependent-variable path.
confusion: Solving for a derivative requires checking the relevant partial derivative is nonzero.

name: mixed partial derivative
quick: A partial derivative taken successively with respect to different inputs.
definition: A partial derivative taken successively with respect to different inputs.
example: For $f=x^2y$, differentiating in x then y gives $f_{xy}=2x$.
confusion: Equality of mixed partials is justified by regularity conditions, not notation alone.

name: Hessian matrix
quick: The matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function.
definition: The matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function.
example: For $x^2+3y^2$, the Hessian is diagonal with entries two and six.
confusion: A Hessian at one point is local information; zero curvature there does not imply a constant function.

name: stationary point
quick: An interior point at which every first partial derivative is zero.
definition: An interior point at which every first partial derivative is zero.
example: The origin is stationary for both $x^2+y^2$ and $x^2-y^2$.
confusion: The zero-gradient condition is necessary for a differentiable interior extremum, not sufficient.
section: Stationary points and the second derivative test

name: inconclusive curvature test
quick: A second derivative test whose zero discriminant leaves the point unclassified.
definition: A second derivative test whose zero discriminant leaves the point unclassified.
example: At the origin, $x^4+y^4$ has a minimum even though its Hessian is zero.
confusion: Inconclusive does not mean that there is no extremum.

name: global multivariable extremum
quick: A smallest or largest function value over the entire stated feasible set.
definition: A smallest or largest function value over the entire stated feasible set.
example: For $x^2+y^2$ on a closed rectangle, compare interior, edge, and corner candidates.
confusion: An excluded boundary point can determine a supremum without attaining a maximum.
section: Global extrema require the whole feasible set

name: double integral
quick: A limit of sums of function values times small areas over a plane region.
definition: A limit of sums of function values times small areas over a plane region.
example: Integrating a constant height three over an area of two gives volume six.
confusion: A double integral is not the square of a single integral.

name: iterated integral
quick: An integral evaluated by integrating one coordinate and then the remaining coordinate.
definition: An integral evaluated by integrating one coordinate and then the remaining coordinate.
example: In $\int_0^2\int_0^1(x+2y)\,dy\,dx$, integrate y first while holding x fixed.
confusion: The inner differential determines the first integration variable.

name: variable integration bounds
quick: Inner limits that describe a region boundary as a function of the outer coordinate.
definition: Inner limits that describe a region boundary as a function of the outer coordinate.
example: The triangle $x,y\geq 0$, $x+y\leq 2$ has y limits zero and $2-x$.
confusion: Bounds describe a region; changing them changes the quantity being accumulated.
section: Describe simple regions with variable bounds

name: order of integration
quick: The sequence in which coordinates are integrated, together with bounds describing the same region.
definition: The sequence in which coordinates are integrated, together with bounds describing the same region.
example: The region $0\leq x\leq y\leq 1$ can be sliced vertically or horizontally.
confusion: Swapping dx and dy without changing dependent bounds generally describes the wrong region.
section: Reverse order by redescribing the same region

name: area average
quick: The integral of a function over a positive-area region divided by that area.
definition: The integral of a function over a positive-area region divided by that area.
example: An integral of twelve over an area of three gives average four.
confusion: Dividing by a side length instead of area gives the wrong average.

name: feasible set
quick: The inputs satisfying every constraint in an optimization problem.
definition: The inputs satisfying every constraint in an optimization problem.
example: The equations x+y=6 with x,y nonnegative describe a line segment.
confusion: An unconstrained optimizer may not be an allowed input.

name: constraint substitution
quick: Eliminating a variable using a constraint while retaining all allowed branches and domain restrictions.
definition: Eliminating a variable using a constraint while retaining all allowed branches and domain restrictions.
example: With x+y=6, replace y by 6-x and optimize the resulting one-variable function.
confusion: Solving with one square-root branch may discard feasible points.
section: Use substitution when it simplifies the problem

name: Lagrange multiplier
quick: A scalar making the objective gradient a multiple of a nonzero constraint gradient at a constrained stationary point.
definition: A scalar making the objective gradient a multiple of a nonzero constraint gradient at a constrained stationary point.
example: For $x^2+2y^2$ with x+y=6, the candidate (4,2) has multiplier 8.
confusion: The multiplier equations are necessary candidate conditions, not by themselves a global-optimality proof.
section: Set up and solve the Lagrange equations

name: constrained extremum comparison
quick: Evaluating an objective at every feasible candidate and relevant boundary point to identify its extrema.
definition: Evaluating an objective at every feasible candidate and relevant boundary point to identify its extrema.
example: On a quarter unit circle, compare the interior product maximum with both arc endpoints.
confusion: Discarded branches and omitted endpoints can hide the global optimum.

name: regular constraint point
quick: A point where the gradient of the equality constraint is nonzero.
definition: A point where the gradient of the equality constraint is nonzero.
example: The line x+y=2 is regular for g=x+y, but its squared equation has zero gradient on the line.
confusion: A zero constraint gradient invalidates the basic multiplier theorem at that point.
section: Recognize singular constraints and modeling limits

name: gradient descent
quick: An iterative method that subtracts a positive multiple of the current objective gradient from the parameter vector.
definition: An iterative method that subtracts a positive multiple of the current objective gradient from the parameter vector.
example: At gradient (4,8) with step size 1/4, the update displacement is (-1,-2).
confusion: Use the same old parameter vector for every gradient component in one update.
section: Take a step using the current gradient

name: gradient descent step size
quick: The positive scalar controlling how far an update moves along the negative gradient.
definition: The positive scalar controlling how far an update moves along the negative gradient.
confusion: Overshooting can still converge; the error magnitude, not only its sign, determines this quadratic behavior.
section: Understand step sizes through an exact recurrence

name: convex function
quick: A function on a convex domain whose value on each segment is at most the corresponding interpolation of endpoint values.
definition: A function on a convex domain whose value on each segment is at most the corresponding interpolation of endpoint values.
example: The function x squared is convex because its graph lies below every chord.
confusion: Convexity does not by itself guarantee a unique minimizer or convergence for every step size.
section: Use convexity to interpret stationary points

name: stationary optimization iterate
quick: An iterate where the objective gradient is zero and an ordinary gradient-descent update therefore makes no movement.
definition: An iterate where the objective gradient is zero and an ordinary gradient-descent update therefore makes no movement.
example: The origin is stationary for $(x^2-1)^2+y^2$ but is a saddle.
confusion: A zero update or small gradient is not a general proof of a minimum.
section: Recognize nonconvex behavior and stopping limits

name: least-squares gradient
quick: For half the squared residual norm, the gradient is the design matrix transpose times the residual vector.
definition: For half the squared residual norm, the gradient is the design matrix transpose times the residual vector.
confusion: Check the loss normalization: omitting the one-half factor doubles the gradient.
section: Connect the gradient to least-squares fitting
